title: Nineveh turns (Jonah 3)
hook: the enemy city repents, down to the cattle, and God relents

segments.voice: Yesterday, inside the great fish, Jonah finally prayed, and gave thanks before he was out. Your line was prayer from the belly. Did you speak honestly from a low moment? Day four hundred eighty-seven.

Chapter three opens with a line that's almost funny in its patience. In the King James Bible: "And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time." The second time. Same message, same city, as if the storm and the fish were just a long detour. And this time Jonah goes. Nineveh is huge, the story says, a city of three days' journey. Jonah walks one day in, stops, and delivers a sermon so short it barely counts. In Hebrew it's five words. In English: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." No call to repent. No promise of mercy. No altar call. Just the warning. And then he waits to see what happens.

Then this: "So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them." The great city of the empire Israel feared turns. All of it, and fast. The news reaches the king. He gets up off his throne, takes off his royal robe, puts on sackcloth and sits in the ash. Then he issues a decree, no person and no animal is to eat or drink. Cattle and sheep too, covered in sackcloth, crying out. It's a little comic, cows in mourning clothes, but it's also complete. The whole city, down to the barn. The king's reasoning is humble: "Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?" Who can tell. He doesn't presume. And then: "God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." And God relented and did not destroy them. Jewish tradition calls this kind of turning teshuvah, coming back, and on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the book of Jonah is read aloud in synagogue. Christians in some churches hear it in Lent. And some readers hear a quiet twist in Jonah's five words: the Hebrew word for overthrown can also mean turned over, changed. In forty days, Nineveh would be turned upside down. It was. Just not the way Jonah meant.
screen: then, large: `WHO CAN TELL IF GOD WILL TURN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: believe someone can change. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've quietly written off. Maybe someone who hurt you, someone whose politics drive you crazy, someone you've decided is just like that. Your own private Nineveh. Hold their face for a moment. You don't have to like them. You don't have to trust them yet. Just ask the king's question: who can tell? Imagine, for a few breaths, that they might turn. What would it look like? If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. If you don't, simply leave the door to their changing open a crack. The bell holds the time.
Nineveh turns. The great enemy city hears five words and turns around, from the king to the cattle, and God relents.
Your line: even nineveh. Today, when you catch yourself saying someone will never change, add three words: who can tell? Day four hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches read Jonah 3 during Lent as a picture of repentance, and Jesus points to the people of Nineveh in Matthew 12:41 and Luke 11:32 as people who turned when they heard Jonah.

fork.setup: you're the king of Nineveh, ruler of a feared empire. a foreign prophet walks in and says your city will be overthrown in forty days. what do you do?
options: take off your robe, sit in ashes, and call a fast.
fork.reveal: the king rises from his throne, puts on sackcloth, sits in ash, and calls the whole city, animals included, to fast and turn. God relents.

original.note: Hebrew: turning, return. the later Jewish word for repentance, the turning Nineveh does.

trapdoor: what you thought: the bad city gets scared and says sorry.
what it means: the enemy Israel feared turns completely, king to cattle, and God's mercy reaches them too.
what a scholar hears: Jonah's word for overthrown can also mean turned over or changed, so his warning came true in an unexpected way.

notes: Jonah's sermon is five words in Hebrew (od arba'im yom v'Nineveh nehpakhet). Confirm the count.
The double sense of the root h-p-k (overthrow / turn, change) is noted by many commentators; confirm it is fairly stated.

teshuvah as a later (rabbinic) term for repentance, related to the verb shuv used in Jonah 3:8–10. Original game uses it; confirm spelling and that it is appropriate on the Christian path as a neighbor's word.
Jewish reading of Jonah at Yom Kippur minchah and Christian Lenten reading mentioned side by side without ranking.
'A three days' journey' (3:3) rendered as 'a three days' walk across'. Confirm.

Editor pass (y2 review): 'The capital of the empire' reintroduced the anachronism day 485's audit removed (Nineveh became capital under Sennacherib); now 'the great city'. Cut 'the shortest sermon in the Bible', 'most deserving of fire' (a ranking of the Ninevites), 'the detail people remember', and 'for exactly this chapter's sake' (an unsourced reason for the Yom Kippur reading). The overthrown/turned double sense is now attributed to 'some readers'. 'Three days' walk across' now follows the KJV 'three days' journey'.
